title: Questions it must keep answering
desc: Turn a real answer into a test, read the verdicts, and stop trusting your memory of last week.
learningGoal: After this lesson you can build a small test set for your own agent and read a row that is not green correctly — telling a real failure apart from one the run could not check.

steps.title: A net, not a demo
steps.bodyMd:
Marloes at Van Dijk Groep built **Inkoopassistent** in the previous chapters: the agent that answers questions about supplier contracts and the price list. It is hers — she wrote its instructions, chose its tools and pressed Publish. Its answers, though, come out of **Inkoopvoorwaarden**, the knowledge base Sandra in procurement keeps up to date. Two people, two objects.

Which is why, two weeks later, nobody can say whether it still answers the cancellation-notice question the way it did. Marloes rewrote two lines of the instructions; Sandra replaced a supplier agreement in the base. Neither of them saw the other's change.

A **test set** is the answer to that. It is a handful of questions plus what a good answer has to contain, stored on the agent. Press **Run** and each question is replayed through the agent's real runtime: the real instructions, the real knowledge, the real tools. A test against a pretend agent proves nothing about the one people talk to.

You will find it on the **Test** tab, in a card called **"Test set"** — *"Questions this agent should keep answering well"*.

steps.question: Sandra replaces a supplier agreement in Inkoopvoorwaarden on Monday. Marloes has not touched Inkoopassistent for two weeks. What does running her test set on Tuesday tell her?

choices.label: How the published agent answers today — its own instructions, plus the base as it now stands. A row can turn red because of a change she never made.
Nothing new: a test set only reacts to edits Marloes makes to the agent itself.
choices.feedback: The run goes through the real runtime, and the real runtime reads the real knowledge. Sandra's Monday document is what the agent answers from on Tuesday — which is exactly the kind of drift a test set exists to catch.

choices.label: Every row comes back blocked, because the knowledge base belongs to someone else.
choices.feedback: Blocked is about capability the sandbox withholds — anything that sends, any routine, anything set to Confirm first. Reading a linked base is none of those.

choices.label: It answers from the documents as they were when Marloes published v2, so Monday's change is invisible until she publishes again.
choices.feedback: Publishing a version fixes the agent's own configuration — instructions, tools, which bases are linked. It does not freeze a copy of the documents inside those bases.

steps.explanation: Ownership is split on purpose here: Marloes owns the agent, Sandra owns the base it reads. A test set is the only thing that notices when the half you do not own moves.

steps.title: Two expectations, two kinds of judge
steps.bodyMd:
A test question carries a **Question**, an optional **Name**, and the expectations. Two of them do the work, and they are graded in completely different ways.

- **Must get across** — *"One per line. A paraphrase counts — this one is judged by an AI, not matched word for word."* So Marloes writes *three months, in writing*, and an answer saying "you have to cancel in writing, three months ahead" still passes.
- **Must never say** — *"One per line, matched word for word."* If the forbidden text is literally in the answer, that is a failure no grader can talk its way out of.

Two more fields finish the picture: **Should use these tools** and **Anything else**.

steps.title: Start from an answer you liked
steps.bodyMd:
The cheapest test to write is one you have already seen work. Ask the agent a real question, like Marloes' *"Wat is de opzegtermijn bij Heijmans Staal?"*, and turn that answer into a test.

An AI reads that one answer and proposes what the test should expect. The dialog says so out loud: **"An AI read that answer and proposed what this test should expect. Read it before you save — it becomes what the test guards."** Fields it wrote carry the chip **"AI wrote this"**.

The proposal is deliberately narrow. It may fill **Must get across** and **Anything else**. **Should use these tools** is not an opinion at all — *"Taken from the tools this chat showed running"* — so trim it to what you really want to require. Nothing exists until you press **Save as test**.

steps.question: Why does the proposal never fill in "Must never say" for you?

choices.label: A prohibition is a rule you decide, not something a model can read out of one answer — and matched word for word, a guessed one turns red for something nobody forbade.
The field only becomes available once the agent has been published.
choices.feedback: It is there from the first test you write. What changes is who fills it: you, always.

choices.label: The AI is not allowed to read the agent's answer, so it has nothing to go on.
choices.feedback: It does read the answer — that is exactly how it proposes "Must get across". The limit is on what it may propose, not on what it may read.

choices.label: "Must never say" is judged by an AI anyway, so a written proposal would be ignored.
choices.feedback: The opposite. "Must get across" is the AI-judged one where a paraphrase counts; "Must never say" is matched word for word.

steps.explanation: The product states it in the field's own help text: "Nothing is proposed here — a prohibition is a rule you write." A literal match is the strictest expectation of the set, so it is the one that must come from a person.

steps.title: A run may lose capability, never gain permission

steps.question: Marloes published v2, then made five edits to Inkoopassistent without publishing. She presses Run. What is being tested?

choices.label: The published agent, v2 — and the run says so, noting how many unpublished changes her draft is ahead.
Her draft, because she is standing in the editor with the draft open.
choices.feedback: The run goes through the real runtime, and once a version is published the runtime serves that published configuration. Her five edits reach nobody yet — not colleagues, and not the test run.

choices.label: Both: each question is asked once against the draft and once against v2, and the row shows the two scores.
choices.feedback: Each question is asked exactly once, through one configuration. There is a single score per row.

choices.label: Nothing runs until she publishes a new version; the button refuses with a warning.
choices.feedback: It runs perfectly well. That is precisely why the screen keeps saying which version answered — a green score on v2 is not a verdict on the draft you are about to ship.

steps.explanation: The screen is honest about it: "This answer came from the published agent, not from your draft." and "Live is v{version}, with {count} unpublished changes." A stale pass presented as a verdict is worse than no test at all — so test, then publish.

steps.title: Four outcomes, and only two are about your agent
steps.bodyMd:
After a run the card shows **"{passed} of {total} passed"**, and each question carries a verdict.

- **pass** — *"Met the expectations in the last run."*
- **fail** — the agent fell short: *"Did not get across everything this test asks for."* or *"Said something this test forbids: …"*. This is the row you act on.
- **blocked** — the run withheld what the test needed, so the agent never had a chance. Not a failure: change the test, or check that tool in a real chat.
- **error** — *"There was no answer to grade, so this says nothing about the agent."*

Only a pass counts towards the green number. A refusal — *"No AI model is set up to grade these answers, so nothing was tested."* — is drawn as a refusal and leaves the score alone, rather than painting your agent red.

steps.title: The loop, in order
steps.instruction: Put the six moves of a working test cycle in the order Marloes uses them.

items.label: Ask the agent a real question and read the answer you get
Turn that answer into a test — read the proposal, then Save as test
Press Run and wait for "{passed} of {total} passed"
Open the row that is not green and read why it is not green
Change the agent: its instructions, its knowledge or its tools
Run the set again, and only then publish a new version

sim.feedback: Both ends matter. A test starts from an answer you have actually seen, because you are the only one who knows what mattered in it. And the rerun comes before the publish, not after — a test set you run after shipping only tells you what you already broke.

steps.title: Build a two-question set and run it
steps.instruction: Open your own agent and ask it two questions a colleague would really ask. Turn each answer into a test with "This conversation as a test": on the first, leave one line under "Must get across"; on the second, add one line under "Must never say" — something this agent has no business saying. Save both, then press Run on the Test tab and read the score and the reasons.

steps.title: What the history remembers
steps.bodyMd:
Press **View** on the card and, under the questions, **Earlier runs** keeps the scores over time — because one number without a history turns a lucky green run into a fact. Four things worth knowing:

- Only the last **20** runs are kept per agent; older ones are pruned.
- A run that stopped part-way is not stored at all — *"What you see below is what had already been tested."* A partial "3 of 3 green" would be the most misleading row here.
- Every stored run remembers which configuration it exercised: **"about v2"** plus **"5 unpublished changes since"**.
- Edit a question afterwards and the row admits it: *"A question changed after this run, so the score is about the older wording."*

An agent holds at most **100** questions, and one press of Run covers at most **25**.

steps.title: What you can do now
steps.bodyMd:
- **Write a test from a real answer.** Ask, like the answer, save it — and read the AI's proposal before you save, because it becomes what the test guards. "Must never say" stays yours.
- **Read a row instead of a number.** A fail is your agent; a blocked row is the run withholding a sending tool, a routine or a confirm-first action; an error is no answer to grade. Only pass is green.
- **Run when someone else's half moves too.** Marloes owns the agent, Sandra owns Inkoopvoorwaarden; a run reads the base as it stands today, so the set catches a document change as readily as an instruction change.
- **Run before you publish.** Once a version is live, the run exercises the published agent — so the score you want is the one taken just before you press Publish new version.

practiceTopic.title: Agent test sets
practiceTopic.summary: Writing test questions for an agent, what the sandbox withholds, and how to read a run.
facts: The Test tab holds a card called "Test set", subtitled "Questions this agent should keep answering well"; empty it reads "No questions yet — turn an answer you liked into the first one."
"Must get across" is judged by an AI and a paraphrase counts; "Must never say" is matched word for word, and nothing is ever proposed for it because a prohibition is a rule you write.
A test run withholds every action that sends, every routine, and every action set to "Confirm first"; write actions still run, and the conversation is never kept.
A test whose expected tool was withheld comes back as blocked, not failed: "A test run never uses {names}, so this could not be checked."

Once a version is published, a run exercises the published agent, not the draft ("This answer came from the published agent, not from your draft.") — and it reads the linked knowledge bases as they stand now, because a version fixes which bases are linked, not a copy of their documents.
Only the last 20 runs are kept per agent, and a run that did not finish is not stored at all.
An agent holds at most 100 test questions, and one press of Run covers at most 25 of them.
The four per-question outcomes are pass, fail, blocked and error, and only pass counts towards "{passed} of {total} passed".

actionChecks.label: Run a test set
actionChecks.hint: In Studio → Agents, open one of your own agents, turn two of its answers into tests, then press Run on the Test tab.

endpoints.returns: array of the agents the caller owns (plus the shared system agents) with id, name, owner_id

criteria.label: One of your agents has at least two test questions
criteria.hint: Add a second question before running — one set of expectations is not a net.
criteria.rule: for some agent the caller owns in GET /agents, GET /agents/:id/tests returns tests.length >= 2
